**Course source:** Day 2 §7. **Running system:** Product, Order and User services.

## From circuit breaking to traffic governance

The source introduces **Sentinel** as a Hystrix alternative and compares their isolation, throttling, exception-rate and response-time approaches. Sentinel's focus includes protecting named resources with configurable flow, degradation and system rules.

In the shop, the important resource is not simply the whole Order process. Different routes have different costs: listing products may be cheap, while checkout may require validation and persistence.

## Define resource and rule separately

~~~text
Resource: order.create
Rule:     admit no more than a configured workload
Action:   reject or degrade excess requests
~~~

The rule should be supported by measurements. A fixed 50-request/s cap may be safe for one environment and too restrictive for another; response-time and concurrency limits can be more meaningful for expensive work.

## Distinguish limiting from breaking

A **rate limiter** controls incoming demand even when dependencies are healthy. A **circuit breaker** reacts to degradation or failure to protect a dependency. A **bulkhead** protects finite concurrency or resources. Sentinel can express different kinds of protection rules, but these concepts should not be collapsed into one word.

## Central dashboard considerations

The course connects applications to Sentinel's console and explores protecting generic resources, REST calls and Feign clients. A dashboard is a control plane. Protect its access, verify that rules are actually applied to instances, and observe how behaviour changes when the control plane is unavailable.

## Minimal mental experiment

At 200 new checkout requests per second, a downstream Product dependency can sustainably handle only 80. Admission control before expensive work reduces the chance of accumulating a large backlog. But rejecting 120 requests/s affects the customer experience and needs an explicit response policy.

## Modern comparison

Sentinel remains a distinct ecosystem choice; Spring Cloud CircuitBreaker/Resilience4j is another route. Compare operational maturity and requirements rather than treating a course's replacement narrative as a timeless ranking.

[Sentinel project](https://github.com/alibaba/Sentinel) · [Spring Cloud CircuitBreaker](https://docs.spring.io/spring-cloud-circuitbreaker/reference/index.html).

## Mathematical Abstraction

A rate limiter caps admitted demand by a policy threshold.

$$
\lambda_{\rm admitted}(t)\leq\min\bigl(\lambda_{\rm offered}(t),\lambda_{\max}(t)\bigr)
$$

This is a fluid-rate approximation; token buckets can allow bursts within an interval, so pointwise instantaneous rates may exceed a long-run refill rate.
